Limited fiscal space, high capital costs, small markets, and the absence of economies of scale continue to slow deployment of renewable energy and progress on energy efficiency. Climate finance must therefore be elevated as a central enabler of the energy transition alongside reforms that improve access to finance and provide instruments that do not exacerbate debt vulnerabilities. International cooperation must also help overcome the unique barriers facing SIDS, including through support for energy system planning, regional and bulk procurement initiatives, and greater accessibility and affordability of renewable energy, battery storage, and energy efficiency technologies. This is precisely the kind of just and equitable transition envisaged under the outcomes of the first Global Stocktake. Today, renewable energy technologies are more affordable than ever before. We have the technologies and we have the agreed global framework. What remains is the political will and the finance to implement them at the speed and scale that science demands. Madam President, for SIDS, the global energy transition is inseparable from the climate agenda. Success will be measured not only in energy security, but lives protected, communities preserved, culture sustained, and the continued ways of life of our people. Let us rise to the urgency of this moment to accelerate the global energy transition and keep 1.5 within reach for our people, our planet, and our future generations. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Palau on behalf of SIDS. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the European Union on behalf of the EU and its member states.

President of the General Assembly, Excellencies, colleagues, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the EU and its member states. We meet at a defining moment for the global energy transition. 10 years after the Paris Agreement entered into force, the world has made important progress, but it remains far from the pace and scale required to keep 1.5 Celsius within reach. This challenge before us is clear: to turn commitment into implementation. The UAE Consensus set out a shared direction to triple global renewable energy capacity, double energy efficiency by 2030, and transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems in a just, orderly, and equitable manner. Our collective task now is to deliver. In this effort, the European Union is playing a leading role at home, with partners, and in multilateral cooperation. Within the European Union, the energy transition is being advanced through ambitious climate and energy legislation, large-scale deployment of renewable energy, stronger energy efficiency measures, and investment in grids storage, and innovation. The US has demonstrated that climate action, competitiveness, and energy security can and must go hand in hand. The recent energy crisis only reinforced this lesson. It exposed the vulnerabilities of the fossil fuel dependence while accelerating efforts across Europe to diversify energy sources reduce demand and scale up clean domestically produced energy. But Europe's responsibility does not stop at its own borders. If we are serious about energy transition, we must do more to support partner countries, especially in Africa and in fragile contexts. At the London Climate Action Week, the EU joined forces with COP31 and COP32 presidents agencies and other partner countries to expand electrification and reduce methane emissions. Through Global Gateway, the EU supports sustainable, high-quality, and trusted investments that connect energy with transport, digital, health, education, water, jobs, and local value creation. By investing in clean energy alongside grids, storage, connectivity, skills, governance, and resilient local systems, we aim to maximize positive spillovers for communities, strengthen reliance, and ensure that the green transition also supports poverty reduction, gender equality, climate action, and sustainable growth. The European Union stands ready to continue working with all partners to accelerate progress. Let this dialogue help move us from intention to implementation, from fragmented efforts to stronger cooperation, and from uneven progress to shared momentum. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of the European Union on behalf of the EU and its member states. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Australia on behalf of the MIKTA. MICTA group, followed by Mexico and Indonesia.

President, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the MICTA countries: Mexico, Indonesia, Republic of Korea, Türkiye, and Australia. MICTA countries are united in our strong commitment to the goals of the Paris Agreement, a decade after its entry into force. We note with concern worsening climate change impacts across the globe, and reaffirm the urgent need to keep 1.5 degrees within reach through nationally determined pathways that support just, orderly, and equitable transitions. We acknowledge the importance of clean energy for the resilience of countries in Southeast Asia and the Pacific, as well as the Mediterranean. We will work together to strengthen regional energy security, including advance— through advancing the energy transition. Recent global energy shocks have reinforced the urgency of accelerating the clean energy transition, which is enhancing energy security, affordability, reliability, and resilience. We must continue to work together to strengthen energy supply chain resilience, including by deepening cooperation and accelerating the transition to clean, affordable, and reliable energy. Clean energy and electrification supported by adequate investment, technology, infrastructure, and capacity building, and rules-based trade is proven and cost-effective, delivering emissions reductions while supporting economic growth, jobs, and industrial development. We underline the importance of implementing these commitments through strengthened international cooperation, capacity building, and enhanced access to climate finance. MIKTA countries remain committed to our net-zero emissions targets, strengthening the multilateral system and promoting investment in clean and renewable energy industries, as recently reaffirmed in our respective NDCs under the Paris Agreement. We encourage all countries who have not yet done so to submit NDCs, National Adaptation Plans, and biennial transparency reports in 2026 to allow Paris Agreement parties to share lessons learned, identify gaps, mobilize support, showcase their progress to date, and highlight investment opportunities for the transition. Just and inclusive energy transitions are a priority for MICTA. They are crucial to achieving orderly energy transitions in pursuit of the goals of the Paris Agreement, while supporting those facing the disproportionate effects of climate change and the energy crisis, particularly in developing countries and vulnerable groups. This grouping is committed to delivering practical, balanced, and ambitious outcomes which advance global climate action on all fronts at COP31. In particular, Türkiye as the President of COP31 and Australia as COP31 President of Negotiations are working closely together to support an inclusive, transparent, and predictable process that promotes dialogue, builds consensus, and advances implementation in the lead-up to COP31. Australia is also working with Pacific Island countries to deliver the pre-COP and leaders event in Fiji and Tuvalu. Our innovative and unique partnership demonstrates a united purpose to tackle the shared challenge of climate change and keep 1.5 degrees within reach. The urgency of climate action needed in this decisive decade demands dialogue and consensus, and it demands concrete action to advance renewables and energy efficiency, to mobilize investment and climate financing, and to facilitate capacity building. We reiterate our calls for global collaboration to accelerate energy transitions, including electrification enabled by grids, energy storage, and investment in renewable energy, ensuring energy security, affordability, reliability, and resilience. We look forward to a advancing these issues at pre-COP, COP31, and beyond.

Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Australia on behalf of the MICTA Group, and this is a session of learning from each other, so we learned also, even though I just Googled and it's already from 2013, but MICTA Group, but so Mexico and Indonesia, the countries I just mentioned, part of the group: Mexico, Indonesia, Republic of Korea, Türkiye, and Australia. So the next The next speaker is not Mexico but France, followed by Morocco and Brazil. And thank you for the important input.

Madam President, Excellencies, France would like to thank you for organizing this dialogue at an important moment, 10 years after the entry into force of the Paris Agreement, we are able to measure progress so far. Investments in renewable technologies are now a lot higher than what is invested in fossil fuels. But this progress is not yet enough given the emergency. We aren't yet on an emissions trajectory that is compatible with keeping global warming below 1.5 degrees. The first global stocktake of the Paris Agreement adopted at COP28 set out a clear roadmap. We need to triple global capacity for renewable energy, double the speed of energy efficiency gains by 2030, and start a transition away from fossil fuels to achieve net zero in 2050. Thank you. To achieve this, there are 3 key priorities. Firstly, accelerating investments in electricity grids, storage, energy efficiency, and the necessary infrastructure for clean electricity, because without modern and resilient grids, capacities for renewable energy and other carbon-neutral energy such as nuclear energy will not be would not be deployable. Secondly, bridging the funding deficit for developing countries. We need to leverage all available financial resources, mobilizing more national financing, strengthening the role of multilateral development banks, and through creating an environment that encourages private investment. Thirdly, making the energy transition a tool for development, energy security, and shared prosperity. Renewable energy will reduce the dependence on fossil fuels, will strengthen resilience to geopolitical crises, and will also create sustainable jobs. France is fully committed to this effort. We are indeed continuing to implement our 3rd national energy transition strategy. This was launched on the 15th of July. And we also are supporting our partners, particularly via Partnerships for Just Energy Transitions. As we approach COP31 in Turkey— Türkiye, we call on member states to present ambitious, credible NDCs that are fully in line with the 1.5°C goal. And here I wish to recall the importance of using the best available scientific data, for example, what's provided by the IPCC. The energy transition is not only a climate necessity— the speaker's microphone has been cut off.

I thank the distinguished representative of France. As we have now members speaking on behalf of the national capacity, the speaking time is 3 minutes. You will see it on screen. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Morocco, followed by Brazil and India.

Thank you, President. My delegation would like to express its gratitude to you for convening this timely and relevant dialogue. In this connection, Morocco would like to make 3 points. Firstly, the energy— current energy context means that we should accelerate the transition rather than slowing it down. Clean energy that is affordable is now a pillar for resilience, energy security, and economic sovereignty when faced with the vulnerabilities that were shown by the dependency on fossil fuels. This has led His Majesty the King of Morocco to put the energy transition at the heart of his development strategy. At the end of 2024, energy— renewable energy was more than 45% of our electricity capacity, which means that we're on track to go beyond our goal of 52% by by 2030. And we have a lot of projects on wind energy and investments in green hydro energy and renewable energy more broadly. Secondly, this technology needs to have solid institutions behind it as well as credible funding. Morocco has strengthened its regulatory framework to foster private investment and integrate renewable energy into the grid. We have a new climate finance strategy for 2030 and our Green taxonomy will also strengthen transparency and reduce the risk of laundering, of greenwashing. Thirdly, we need access to financing to pay particular attention to adaptation. Africa, unfortunately, only has 2% of global investments in clean energy, whereas we have 60% of the solar capacity. So the high cost of capital means there is insufficient access to concessional financing, and this is undermining the deployment of renewable energy still. COP31 should make financial pledges more concrete, particularly the roadmap towards $1.3 trillion, but— and it should also make the market's mechanisms more operational and attract necessary investment for national contributions. Multilateral banks should drive and attract private capital in local currency, and climate funds should simplify the procedures and accelerate the payments that they make. We remain, Madam President, completely committed to climate action, as His Majesty the King highlighted at COP28, and it is urgent to go beyond simply taking small steps, but we need to take— we need to show goodwill and an enlightened vision. This vision should guide us towards COP31, that is an ambitious COP. Thank you very much indeed.
I thank the distinguished representative of Morocco. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Brazil.

Thank you, Excellencies. Well, Madam President, Excellencies, colleagues, I thank the PGA for organizing this debate. I must start by expressing Brazil's concern with narratives that seek to downplay the need to accelerate the renewable energy transition. The energy sector remains responsible for approximately 80% of global greenhouse gas emissions, and the growing global demand for electricity must be met with sustainable and affordable energy. Multilateralism and international cooperation are essential to advancing a just, orderly, and equitable energy transition. The UN, through its universal membership, legitimacy, and convening power, remains the cornerstone of international cooperation and an indispensable forum for dialogue and collective action. This shift in paradigm presents challenges, but also significant opportunities. Recent developments in the Middle East and the resulting volatility in energy markets confirm a fundamental truth: Energy transition is also energy security. Excessive dependence on limited sources, technologies, or suppliers increases vulnerability to geopolitical tensions. Diversification, resilience, and sustainability are therefore strategic imperatives, not only climate objectives. Moving away from fossil fuels requires building lower-carbon— low-carbon, resilient energy sources. Electrification powered by renewables is the principal pathway for power, transport, and buildings, but cannot reach every sector. Aviation, shipping, long-distance transport, and heavy industry will depend on sustainable fuel alternatives for some time. Brazil's experience illustrates this connection. Since the 1973 oil crisis, sustained investment in biofuels has diversified our energy matrix, strengthening energy security while advancing emissions reductions, innovation, rural development, and green jobs. More recently, wind and solar expansion has brought renewables to about 85— I'm sorry, 50% of Brazil's energy mix, with electricity generation close to 90% renewable, proving that decarbonization and security are mutually reinforcing, and compatible with growth and competitiveness. Naturally, transition pathways will differ across countries, reflecting national circumstances and priorities. In all cases, however, international cooperation is indispensable. Colleagues, the energy transition is not a burden, but an opportunity for more resilient, competitive, and sustainable economies. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Brazil.

Madam President, India appreciates the convening of this dialogue as we mark 10 years since the entry into force of the Paris Agreement. The challenge is to ensure that the energy transition will be equitable, just, inclusive, and supportive of sustainable development. We would like to make the following points. First, climate ambition and sustainable development must advance together. Guided by the principles of equity and CBDRRC, countries must retain the policy space to pursue nationally determined pathways that respond to their development priorities while contributing to global climate action. Second, these pathways must contend with contemporary realities. Creating an artificial hierarchy among fossil fuels and demonizing coal while extolling natural gas as the only viable transition fuel is not a feasible option. The ongoing conflict in the Middle East has exposed deep structural geopolitical and supply chain constraints that obviate entirely relying on LNG for this purpose, especially for Asia that does not have pipeline supplies. Global South has to rely on energy sources that are domestically available, are affordable and accessible through global supply chains that do not shut due to structural or geopolitical reasons. Third, access to technology is vital while pursuing our ambitious climate targets. India is investing in coal gasification and green hydrogen alongside carbon capture, utilization, and storage. India has set itself an ambitious target of 500 gigawatts of installed non-fossil electricity capacity by 2030, and solar energy is expected to contribute a large share in this target. As of last month, India has already installed over 162 gigawatts of solar capacity, making it one of the world's largest solar markets. Developed countries must fulfill their commitments on the provision of finance, technology development and transfer, and capacity building. Fourth, energy transition must remain fair and inclusive. Unilateral measures such as carbon border adjustment mechanisms that transfer the cost of decarbonization to developing countries or serve as disguised restrictions on international trade make no sense in today's context of supply chain, tariff, and other trade-related uncertainties, with the WTO rules-based trade regime in dysfunction. Fifth, the General Assembly should complement and not duplicate the work undertaken under the UNFCCC and its Paris Agreement. Climate negotiations are conducted by parties in the dedicated intergovernmental processes established under UNFCCC, where the principles of equity and CBDRRC are firmly embedded. Discussions in the General Assembly should therefore focus on facilitating implementation, promoting international cooperation, sharing best practices, and supporting capacity building, while respecting the mandates, processes, and outcomes of the UNFCCC and avoiding the creation of parallel negotiating tracks or reinterpretation of agreed commitments. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of India. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom.

Thank you, President, Excellencies, colleagues. We meet at a decisive moment. As we've heard today, the global energy transition is no longer a question of whether change is coming. The question is whether we can build quickly enough, to invest wisely enough, and to work together effectively enough to ensure that change delivers for our people. At COP28, we agreed to triple global renewable energy capacity. to double the rate of energy efficiency improvement and transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems in a just, orderly, and equitable manner. At COP31 in Antalya, our task is clear: to turn that consensus into implementation. Clean energy investment is set to reach $2.2 trillion this year. That's a significant opportunity. But we must ensure that investment reaches the countries that need it most, helping to lower costs, to expand access to clean power, and unlock sustainable growth. This is not only a climate agenda. Recent energy shocks have exposed the economic and security risks that come with dependence on volatile fossil fuel markets. Clean power, greater efficiency, and electrification can strengthen energy security security. It can improve affordability and support jobs, growth, and resilience. Through the Global Clean Power Alliance, the Green Grids Initiative, Just Energy Transition Partnership, and Mission 300, the United Kingdom is working with partners to mobilize finance to strengthen grids and storage and to turn clean power ambitions into scalable, investable projects. Our focus is practical. It's about removing barriers to delivery and translating commitments into results that people can see, that people can feel: more reliable energy, stronger economies, greater resilience, and enhanced energy security. So, the choice isn't between climate action, growth, and security. Done well, clean energy is one of the clearest pathways to all 3. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cuba Followed by Ecuador and Estonia.

Madam President, Cuba thanks you for convening this interactive dialogue, which is coming at a very timely moment. The transition to renewable sources of energy and increase in energy efficiency are essential in order to tackle climate change and achieve sustainable development. However, in order for this transition to be a truly just one, it must be grounded in the principles of equity, common but differentiated responsibilities, and respective capacities, as well as the full respect for the national priorities and circumstances of developing countries. We can't talk about a global energy transition if we don't address the profound inequalities that persist in access to energy, financing, technology, and the capacity required to undertake this transition. This is why Cuba reiterates the need to strengthen international cooperation and to ensure adequate, predictable, and sustainable access to concessional financing, as well as to technology and capacities. The energy transition must not become a new area of exclusion, nor must it widen existing gaps between developed and developing countries. In this context, it's essential to condemn unilateral coercive measures which block sustainable development and the energy transition of developing countries, such as the United States embargo against Cuba, which is one of the most brutal manifestations of this, that prevents Cuba's access to fuel and essential supplies, with direct consequences for our economy and to the daily lives of our people. These extraterritorial measures also affect third countries and companies that want to cooperate with Cuba. They block investment projects and cooperation projects precisely in the area of renewable energies. Despite these adversities, Cuba maintains its commitment to the energy transition and to developing renewable sources of energy, and we are advancing here by adopting cooperation projects and progressively broadening our participation, the participation of renewable energy in the national energy mix. The energy transition will only be truly global if it's just inclusive and it has solidarity. Cuba will continue to defend a more equitable international order where no country is deprived of their right to development and where cooperation can prevail over coercion. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cuba. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ecuador.

Thank you, Madam President. As long as climate financing gaps persist and as long as developing countries lack timely access to sufficient, predictable, and accessible resources, the energy transition will remain a Pipe dream. Increasing financing must be a priority because a lack of financing is not due to a lack of resources but due to fragmentation, as you mentioned, Madam President. Ecuador has shown that innovative instruments that generate concrete results for the conservation of nature and the protection of biodiversity and resilience to climate change are not sufficiently supported by the international community. And I'll just simply mention 2 examples, 2 successful experiences in the implementation of innovative financing mechanisms for climate action in Ecuador and for the energy transition. And you also mentioned these 2, and thank you for mentioning that. In 2023, we delivered the biggest debt swap that we've seen in nature conservation that enabled us to channel resources to the Galápagos LIFE Fund for financing marine conservation actions. This operation saw approximately $1.6 billion of existing debt swapped for a new loan of $656 million to finance conservation initiatives, marine conservation initiatives over the next 18 years. And this operation is a long-term one and is an example of a commitment to the country to conserving 2 marine ecosystems of global importance, the Galápagos Marine Reserve and the Hermandad Marine Reserve. Then in December 2024, we delivered a new debt conversion that saw a saving of $800 million, of which $460 million were devoted to conserving the Ecuadorian Amazon through the Amazon Biocorridor Program. Recently, a new step of this program was started with the process to build the Amazon Biocorridor Conservation Plan, an instrument that will focus the actions required to achieve the commitments made to conserve these unique ecosystems. They're unique in the whole world. Madam President, distinguished colleagues, These experiences show that it is possible to work towards a sustainable energy transition. Ecuador reiterates its commitment, and we reiterate why adequate financing is required. We have engaged in these actions in our national government that show that we can move from words to practice. Thank you very much, Madam President.

Gracias also for sharing in such detail, and this is in a formal setting, and it's exactly about this, how we can learn from each other, and also maybe if others in the room, because we know that the depth issue is one of the core issues for many investments, could also take this up, where the challenges are, and also ask our experts and distinguished guests at the panel, maybe as a summary, to speak about the hurdles, why things like this are not scaled up on a bigger, bigger, bigger scale. So, thank you very much for sharing. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Estonia, followed by Nepal and Namibia.

Thank you, Madam President. Estonia is firmly committed to achieving climate neutrality by 2050. We support the EU target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 55% by 2030, as well as the goals of tripling renewable energy capacity and transitioning away from fossil fuels, as agreed during COP28 in Dubai. These objectives guide Estonia's climate and energy policies. Compared to 1990, our greenhouse gas emissions have fallen by 66%, largely due to transformation in the energy Once heavily dependent on oil shale, Estonia has rapidly expanded renewables. In the past 5 years, solar power capacity has increased more than 13 times. Wind power capacity has more than doubled, and today around 40% of our electricity consumption comes from domestic renewable sources. Looking ahead, Estonia aims to achieve 80% clean electricity consumption by 2035, mainly through new onshore wind farms providing clean, secure, and affordable energy. Today's volatile energy markets show clearly that dependence on imported fossil fuels is a vulnerability. The fastest and most affordable path forward is greater clean energy production and energy efficiency. Estonia is therefore investing in electricity interconnections with neighboring countries and modern energy infrastructure that strengthens resilience and energy security. Estonia is also a tech nation. Since 2016, the number of Estonian clean tech companies has increased tenfold. We are home to science-based global leaders in energy storage, energy efficiency, sustainable materials, and electrolyzer technologies for hydrogen production. Technologies is a key enabler of a just and inclusive energy transition. Internationally, Estonia remains committed to climate finance and partnerships that support resilience, clean energy access, and forest protection in vulnerable countries. Strengthening the international climate and energy partnerships and continuing climate diplomacy in line with the Paris Agreement are key to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and increasing resilience to climate change. We welcome the recent letter of the COP31 presidency, Türkiye and Australia, which commits to advancing clean energy as a key priority.

I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Estonia. Thank you, Estonia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Nepal, followed by Namibia and Mexico.

Thank you, Madam President. The climate shocks are intensifying at scale and speed worldwide. Despite contributing a negligible share of global greenhouse gas emissions, Nepal remains among the countries most vulnerable to climate change. Our nationally determined contribution and climate frameworks reflect the global ambition to expand renewable energy and contribute to global climate goals. We remain committed to achieving net-zero emissions by 2045 while reducing net greenhouse gas emissions by nearly 17% by 2030 and 27% by 2035. By harnessing our abundant renewable energy resources, particularly hydropower, we aim to generate over 28,000 megawatts of electricity, expand the use of electric cookstoves to more than 2 million households, and ensure that 95% of new private passenger vehicle sales are battery electric vehicles by 2035. Over 95% of our people have access to electricity now. In last fiscal, we earned about USD 190 million from electricity exports that reflect a promising window for our national development and regional energy security. Electric vehicle adoption has risen from just 8% in 2019 to 73% in 2025, ranking Nepal second in EV adoption globally. However, limited storage capacity, seasonal variability in hydropower generation, insufficient transmission and cross-border interconnection infrastructure, affordability gaps for vulnerable communities, and constrained access to predictable long-term financing continue to slow the pace of our energy transition. Let me highlight 3 priorities. First, we must significantly scale up affordable and accessible financing for developing countries, particularly countries in special situations. Investment from climate funds, IFIs, multilateral development banks, development partners, and the private sector are indispensable to expand renewable energy infrastructure, create green jobs, and support a just and inclusive energy transition. For Nepal alone, implementing the NDC 3 mitigation targets requires an estimated USD 74 billion, with around 85% expected from external sources. Meeting our adaptation priorities will require an additional USD 18 to 20 billion. Second, we must fully implement global instruments and commitments to keep 1.5°C pathway on track. The Paris Agreement, COP outcomes, and Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 7, and the recent ICJ Advisory Opinion provide a strong legal and normative foundation for climate action. Nepal co-sponsored the recent UN resolution on ICJ Advisory Opinion on climate change and strongly advocated for the incorporation of commitments to triple renewable energy capacity, double energy efficiency by 2030, and transition away from fossil fuels in a just, orderly, and equitable manner in the resolution. Third, international cooperation must be strengthened to accelerate technology transfer, innovation, capacity building, and knowledge sharing. Developing countries like my own country need equitable access to renewable energy technologies, energy storage solutions, critical energy transition minerals, and modern infrastructure. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Nepal. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Namibia.

Madam President, we commend your initiative to convene this timely dialogue as we mark a decade since the Paris Agreement entered into force. We thank all the briefers for their statements. Namibia is advancing a just and inclusive energy transition by scaling up renewable energy deployment through our Integrated Resource Plan, expanding access to electricity, and creating an environment— enabling environment for investment in solar, wind, and green hydrogen. These efforts are helping to strengthen energy security, create jobs, and support sustainable industrialization while contributing to our climate commitments. We are targeting 70% of renewable energy electricity generation by 2030. Namibia is the world's 3rd largest producer of uranium necessary to support clean nuclear energy production. Moreover, Namibia's abundant renewable solar and wind energy resources have positioned it as a front-runner in the global green hydrogen economy. Namibia's green hydrogen sector has the potential to power sustainable industrialization, foster job creation, and secure its role as a competitive exporter of green energy and derivatives. However, the cost of capital and technology remains high, and developing countries, particularly in Africa, who still rely heavily on fossil fuels for energy and industrialization, need flexibility to pursue their development paths in order to overcome poverty and national challenges. Moreover, the crisis in the Middle East and its impact on energy prices has exposed the world's continued dependence on fossil fuels. Namibia therefore emphasizes that because nations are at different stages of development, the global energy transition must be done in a just, fair, inclusive, responsible, orderly, and equitable manner to ensure that no country is left behind, in line with the international commitments noted in the Pact for the Future. In this regard, and in order to accelerate implementation towards an energy transition There is a need for strengthened partnerships and cooperation towards technology transfer, infrastructure development, concessional finance, blended finance mechanism, risk-sharing instruments, increased investments in grid modernization, regional interconnections, and energy storage. Climate justice must go hand in hand with financial justice.

I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Namibia. I now give floor to the distinguished representative of Mexico, followed by Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Korea. Muchas gracias.

Thank you very much, Madam President. Mexico thanks you for convening this interactive dialogue, which keeps the energy transition at the forefront of the international agenda at a critical moment for climate action. Today, The challenge is to accelerate the implementation of our existing commitments through concrete actions that reflect the different national circumstances, development priorities, and energy realities of each country. Mexico supports a gradual, orderly, just, and inclusive energy transition. We are convinced that it is possible to achieve economic growth, industrialize, and at the same time protect our planet. To this end, climate ambition and energy security must advance hand in hand by strengthening the resilience of our energy systems through the diversification of energy sources, the modernization of infrastructure, and the enhancement of national and regional capacities. The transformation required to keep the 1.5 degrees Celsius goal within reach calls for a long-term vision consistent public policies, appropriate incentives, and regulatory certainty to encourage investment. In this context, strategic public planning remains indispensable to ensure that the expansion of renewable energy, electrification, and emerging technologies serves the public interest and responds to the present and future needs of the energy system. As part of this strategy, Mexico is advancing the development of energy storage technologies, green manufacturing, and the circular economy, while placing energy efficiency at the center of its efforts to strengthen energy security, reduce costs, and deliver tangible benefits for households, industry, and public finances. We also recognize that the transition requires complementary public and private investment. However, for many developing countries, The principal challenge remains access to affordable finance, technology, and institutional capacity. International cooperation must therefore expand access to concessional finance, reduce the cost of capital, and strengthen project preparation while ensuring that private finance complements rather than replaces the essential role of public resources. Finally, Mexico believes that regional cooperation is a key accelerator of the energy transition. Regulatory convergence, regional value chains, technological cooperation, and greater electricity interconnection can strengthen resilience and facilitate access to cleaner energy. We reiterate that greater ambition must be matched by greater means of implementation so that the energy transition effectively contributes to universal access to energy, reduces inequalities, and a better quality of life for all. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Mexico.

Thank you, Madam President, for holding this important dialogue. Energy security is a top priority for Saudi Arabia. Development in international markets confirmed that the current challenges to energy security are not contingent on the type of resource; rather, they are linked to other factors that may affect market stability. Therefore, replacing one reliable energy source with another does not necessarily alleviate these challenges. Rather, it may create a new source of vulnerability. This is why, from our perspective, phasing out or eliminating fossil fuels will weaken the capacity of states and approaches and processes they have chosen to honor their commitments. It could undermine energy security and have significant economic repercussions across the world. Indeed, fossil fuel remains a fundamental component of the global energy mix and will remain so for the next decades. To realize sustainable development in this context, Madam President, we reaffirm that energy security is not limited to diversifying energy sources. It also encompasses the protection of infrastructure, the guarantee of the security of waterways, and the freedom of navigation. Development in the Straits of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb demonstrate the need for increased international cooperation to ensure the continuous, safe, and reliable supply of energy to global markets in compliance, naturally, with international law. And relevant Security Council resolutions. In conclusion, we reiterate that the difference of natural resources and development needs and development necessitate using conventional and renewable energy while allying the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and contributing to the realization of sustainable development. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Saudi Arabia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Republic of Korea, followed by El Salvador and Thailand.

Thank you, Madam President. The global energy transition has become more urgent than ever. The Republic of Korea is tackling this issue by working to increase the share of carbon-free power sources to around 70% by 2038, while pursuing a balanced mix of clean energy sources. We are also advancing offshore wind and hydrogen technologies and promoting digital-based energy efficiency innovation to build a more flexible and resilient energy system. Building on these practices, the Republic of Korea would like to I would like to propose 2 areas of cooperation with the international community. First, we must advance infrastructure investment and local capacity building to expand energy access in developing countries. Many developing countries possess significant renewable energy potential, but to fully exploit these resources, they must overcome challenges including insufficient power grids and infrastructure constraints. The Republic of Korea, together with the African Development Bank, has been supporting energy infrastructure development in Africa since 2021 through the Korea-Africa Energy Investment Framework. To support the scale of these efforts, it's essential to utilize public and concessional resources as catalysts and leverage blended finance to effectively mobilize private capital. Second, we must build mutually beneficial and sustainable critical mineral supply chains to support the transition to clean energy. The Republic of Korea is supporting value creation in resource-rich countries and sustainable critical mineral development through concrete cooperation initiatives, including the Mohenjo-daro graphite project in Tanzania. This reflects the spirit of mutual beneficial cooperation between producing and consuming countries reaffirmed at the 2024 Korea-Africa Summit. Excellencies, energy transition is a challenge that no country can achieve alone. The Republic of Korea remains committed to strengthening international cooperation with the United Nations and member states to advance an inclusive and sustainable energy transition. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Republic of Korea. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of El Salvador.

The transition to clean energy is not only essential for tackling climate change, it is also fundamental for strengthening energy security, enhancing resilience, and creating new opportunities for sustainable economic growth. Denmark stands ready to work with all partners to advance these shared objectives. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Denmark. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Indonesia, followed by Azerbaijan.

Madam President, we thank you for convening this important event as we mark a decade since the Paris Agreement entered into force. We also thank the briefers for their insightful At the outset, Indonesia aligns itself with the joint statement delivered by Australia on behalf of MIKTA. Indonesia wishes to highlight 3 key points. First, for Indonesia, the energy transition must advance climate ambition and sustainable development while safeguarding energy security, affordability, and resilience. It must be guided by equity and the principles of CBDRRC.

Thank you.

Under our 2nd NDC, Indonesia's national emissions are projected to peak by 2030 and decline thereafter towards net-zero emissions by 2060 or sooner. We are translating this commitment into action through our electricity supply business plan for 2025 to 2034. It provides for 69.5 gigawatts of additional capacity, with 74 to 76% coming from new and renewable energy sources and energy storage, supported by expanded and strengthened electricity grids. Second, a just, orderly, and equitable transition must be inclusive and nationally determined, and taking into account national circumstances and development priorities. In terms of financing, Our experience shows that mobilizing investment requires clear policy direction, bankable project pipelines, and effective risk-sharing mechanisms. Since 2022, Indonesia's Energy Transition Mechanism Country Platform has served as a national vehicle for mobilizing blended finance to support early retirement of coal-fired power plants, and investment in clean and renewable energy, such as floating solar projects and hydro infrastructures. Third, international cooperation must move from commitments to implementation, particularly through adequate and accessible climate finance, technology transfer, and capacity building. South-South and triangular cooperation can further scale up practical country-driven solutions. In our region, the ASEAN power grid also demonstrates how cross-border connectivity and multilateral power trade can strengthen energy security and improve resilience. To close, we reiterate the importance of this meeting to complement the work of the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement and help translate agreed commitments into concrete cooperation and delivery. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Indonesia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Azerbaijan, followed by Pakistan and Uruguay.

Thank you, Madam President. At the outset, I would like to thank you for convening this interactive dialogue on accelerating the global energy transition. The transition to clean energy has become a defining element of sustainable development, climate action, and long-term energy security. While important progress has been made in expanding renewable energy and improving energy efficiency, significant challenges remain. In this context, international cooperation and effective partnerships remain indispensable. Azerbaijan believes that cross-border cooperation and multinational partnerships can play an important role in strengthening energy security while advancing global climate objectives. As the COP29 presidency, Azerbaijan has worked to strengthen international cooperation and advance implementation across key areas of climate action. Under the Baku Climate Unity Pact, key breakthroughs were achieved across all pillars, from long-awaited progress on operationalizing high-integrity carbon to agreement on a new collective climate finance goal for the first time in the history of the UNFCCC and making the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage fully operational. Recognizing that the rapid deployment of renewable energy must be accompanied by modern and resilient electricity systems, Azerbaijan also launched the COP29 Global Energy Storage and Grids Pledge initiative, which promotes stronger investment in electricity grids and energy storage as essential enablers of a secure, reliable, and resilient clean energy transition. At the national level, Azerbaijan is pursuing an ambitious energy diversification agenda guided by its National Development Strategy, Azerbaijan 2030: National Priorities for Socioeconomic Development, which identifies building a clean environment and a country of green growth as one of the country's 5 national priorities. In line with this vision, Azerbaijan continues to expand renewable energy generation through large-scale solar, wind, and hydropower projects across different regions, including the liberated territories. Azerbaijan's post-conflict reconstruction and development efforts likewise demonstrate its commitment to green growth and sustainability. Guided by the principles of environment, stewardship and climate resilience. These efforts incorporate renewable energy solutions and innovative smart city and smart village concepts. Madam President, accelerating the global energy transition requires practical action, strengthened partnerships, and sustained investment in renewable energy. Azerbaijan remains committed to advancing clean environment and green growth through its investments in renewable energy. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Azerbaijan. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Pakistan.

Thank you, Madam President, for convening this dialogue. The transition is indeed possible, but it is not easy. Progress remains concentrated in a few regions, with developing countries including ours lagging behind. Recent volatility in global energy markets has illustrated the cost of moving too slowly. As Mr. Steele noted, Pakistan's renewables capacity did soften the impact on our power sector a bit, but for us, this also points to a broader issue of supply chain stability, resilience, and diversification beyond the issue of energy alone. Renewables account for over 30% of Pakistan's power mix, and solar capacity has grown sevenfold since 2021. Our NDC 3.0 targets 62% renewables and hydropower by 2035, 1,200 megawatts of new nuclear by 2030, and efficiency savings of 35 million tons of CO2 equivalent at an estimated cost of $565.7 billion. However, the real question is one of implementation. The central barrier to implementation is finance. The cost of capital for developing countries remains too high. and climate finance still flows overwhelmingly as loans rather than grants, adding to debt burdens. Developed countries must fulfill their climate finance commitments. Fulfillment of the $300 billion NCEQG goal through grant-based finance would help, though it remains insufficient. We also call for adequate replenishment of climate funds and for the tripling of adaptation finance. The cost of capital must be lowered through guarantees, blended finance, and local currency lending, alongside a shift from loans to grants and scaled-up MDB lending with a view to tripling it. We must also speedily implement the commitments under the Compromiso de Sevilla on debt, particularly to convene a dialogue on debt as part of the UN Intergovernmental Process. None of the aforementioned solutions are new. They are existing commitments which have not been implemented. In addition to finance, cost and access to technologies such as storage technologies matters just as much, a gap that hits developing countries hardest given weak technology transfer as well as limited local manufacturing capacity. Grid infrastructure is yet another constraint. In conclusion, a just, orderly, and equitable transition means its costs must not fall disproportionately on developing countries. It must be consistent with the principle of CBDR, and it must allow for flexibilities with pathways that can differ across countries in their pursuit of sustainable development in its 3 dimensions. Climate action must also not become a pretext for new barriers to trade and development. I thank you.

And its derivatives and new productive sectors. The international community, with the UN playing a key role and with support from international financial institutions including the World Bank Group and The international financial cooperation must move towards a more effective financial architecture that broadens access to long-term financing, reduces the cost of capital for developing countries, and mobilizes new private investments through risk mitigation mechanisms and combined financing. Madam President, the energy transition should not be measured only by megawatts installed, but also by its ability to bring about jobs, to promote innovation, and create opportunities for sustainable and inclusive development. Uruguay reaffirms its commitment to share its experiences, to work with all member states to drive forward an accelerated, just energy transition based on renewed international cooperation that mobilizes the investments that the world needs. Thank you very much.

Continue to slow the pace of the transition. In this regard, the Philippines supports stronger partnership among multilateral development banks, international financial institutions, climate funds, bilateral partners, and the private sector. Expanding access to concessional and blended finance, and technical assistance will help mobilize private investment, accelerate grid modernization, and scale up clean energy deployment. Equally important is international cooperation in technology transfer, capacity building, and knowledge sharing. As Chair of ASEAN, the Philippines also recognizes the value of regional cooperation in advancing a secure, resilient, and sustainable energy future. As ASEAN moves forward with the implementation of ASEAN 2045, Our shared future, strengthening regional energy connectivity, expanding renewable energy deployment, and promoting sustainable investment will be essential to accelerating the region's energy transition. As we look ahead to COP31, we must match our collective ambition with stronger implementation by scaling up finance and strengthening technology cooperation and ensuring that countries that have the means to deliver on their commitments. In this regard, The United Nations has an important role in promoting greater coherence across climate action, sustainable development financing, and technology cooperation. Through stronger multilateral partnership, we can help ensure that no country is left behind. The Philippines remains committed to working with all partners to advance a secure, resilient, affordable, and sustainable energy future for all. Thank you, Madam President.

Portugal aligns with the statement delivered by the EU and would like to add the following. 10 years after the entry into force of the Paris Agreement, direction is clear. The challenge is no longer whether the energy transition will happen, but whether we can deliver it at the speed and scale required. The clean energy transition is not only a climate imperative, It is also fundamental for strengthening energy security, enhancing economic resilience, and creating new opportunities for sustainable growth. Recent geopolitical crises have reminded us that reducing dependence on fossil fuels is not only an environmental objective, it is also a strategic one. Implementation must therefore be a priority. This means accelerating renewable energy deployment, modernizing electricity grids, improving energy efficiency, and ensuring that permitting, regulation, and infrastructure keep pace with growing investments. At the same time, we cannot ignore the financing gap. A just and inclusive transition requires stronger multilateral cooperation, a greater mobilization of concessional finance, and development banks that are able to leverage significantly more private investment, particularly to developing countries. Portugal remains committed to contributing to these efforts, both domestically and internationally. Nationally, we continue to accelerate renewable deployment through our updated National Energy and Climate Plan, while investing in storage, green hydrogen, and electrification of transport and industry. Internationally, We believe that innovative partnerships are equally important. Portugal has pioneered debt-for-climate swap mechanisms, redirecting debt repayments into climate and environmental investment. These partnerships demonstrate how tailored financial solutions can strengthen resilience, support sustainable development, and help mobilize additional investment where it is most needed. Looking ahead to COP31, our collective task is clear to translate existing commitments into concrete implementation. We know what needs to be done. The priority is to ensure that all countries have the means to deliver a just and inclusive energy transition.
